title: Leaders Who Awkwardly Overshare About Themselves
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses leaders whose disclosures about their personal lives cross a professional boundary and make colleagues uncomfortable. It distinguishes healthy openness about opinions and views — which builds credibility — from oversharing personal or emotional material, which erodes trust instead. Because oversharing leaders often respond to colleagues' withdrawal by disclosing even more, the article offers team members a specific tactic: validate briefly, then abruptly redirect to a work topic, using sample scripted lines. Over time, repeated redirection teaches the leader where the boundary sits.
points: Distinguishes credibility-building candor about opinions from boundary-crossing disclosure about personal or emotional matters.
Oversharing leaders often misread colleagues' discomfort as distance to be closed with more disclosure, which compounds the problem.
Recommends a specific two-step tactic for team members: briefly validate, then abruptly pivot to a work topic.
Provides scripted example lines team members can reuse to redirect an oversharing conversation without confrontation.
Frames boundary-setting as a repeatable skill leaders can be taught through consistent, gentle redirection over time.
quotes: Some leaders can’t stop themselves from disclosing too much. They make others feel awkward and uncomfortable whenever they share too many personal issues and details.

Leaders who tell others what they really think and feel about issues normally enhance their credibility. We like leaders who are more open and honest about what they think. But this doesn’t apply to their personal lives or deeply held suspicions or complaints.
As people pull away from them, they often feel the need to disclose even more to reestablish their connection. This can make conversations exasperating.
Team members can help leaders who overshare by validating the conversation and then abruptly changing the topic.

By abruptly shifting topics, those on the receiving end draw a boundary line that is difficult to breach. Over time, leaders learn that team members are uninterested in exploring such personal issues further.
